It isn't necessarily bad, but the gameplay is completely different. If you look at Devil May Cry, for instance, you can see how faithful it remained to the gameplay style of its **** short: After 20 years, what I really wanted was a sequel to those wonderful games that defined my childhood—seeing a new hero like Jubei Yagyu save the day. I didn't know the lore or history, but Way of the Sword blew me away from minute one.What Makes It a 10: Zero Lore Barrier: You jump straight into playing as Miyamoto Musashi fighting demon Genma in Kyoto. No homework needed.   Masterful Combat: Fast, fluid, and ridiculously satisfying. Mastering the Issen counter-strike timing makes you feel completely unstoppable.   Epic Bosses: The high-stakes duels test your reflexes and feature some of the best encounter design in modern action gaming.Verdict:You don't need to be a long-time fan to fall in love with this game. If you like samurai action, incredible boss fights, and badass swordplay, this is an absolute must-play.

positive.quote: After two decades of waiting, Capcom has finally brought back one of its most beloved franchises with Onimusha: Way of the Sword. This isn't just a simple nostalgic cash-grab; it is a complete, ground-up reinvention that successfully modernizes the classic samurai action for a new generation. **Story and Presentation**The game follows the journey of a young, cocky, yet highly skilled Miyamoto Musashi in feudal Kyoto. After acquiring the mysterious Oni Gauntlet, Musashi is thrust into a war against the demonic Genma. The narrative is engaging and well-paced, swapping between different character perspectives to keep the player hooked. What truly elevates the presentation is the outstanding character acting. The facial animations and voice acting are top-notch, perfectly capturing Musashi’s witty, sarcastic charm during intense showdowns. **Gameplay and Combat**Capcom has overhauled the gameplay entirely, abandoning the old tank controls and fixed camera angles in favor of fluid, dynamic movement. The combat feels heavy, deliberate, and incredibly fierce. Every sword strike carries immense weight. While it offers deep mechanical depth reminiscent of games like Nioh, it proudly stays true to its action roots rather than forcing itself into the modern "Soulslike" formula. For players struggling with the difficulty, the inclusion of an optional "Action Prompt" system helps teach defensive and counter-attack windows, making the game accessible without reducing the actual challenge. **Performance**True to Capcom's recent track record, the game runs beautifully. Visually, Kyoto looks stunning, and the performance is incredibly stable on both consoles and PC. Aside from minor frame drops when reloading saves—which are easily fixed—the optimization is practically flawless. **Verdict**Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an outstanding revival that honors its roots while bravely carving out a modern identity. With intense combat, an addictive gameplay loop, and excellent storytelling, Capcom has delivered yet another masterpiece in 2026.

negative.quote: Como fan desde pequeño de los onimusha la verdad me he llevado una pequeña decepcion, los enemigos son lentos, los jefes demasiado faciles, es un juego centrado en jugadores casuales. Se convierte demasiado rapido en un juego repetitivo y añadirle ese medio “mundo abierto” de Kyoto no hace mas que restarle, no he llegado ni a mitad del juego y me parece que capcom aqui ha chirriado un poco, no es fiel a los onimushas y mucho menos a un soulslike, es una pena pero no lo recomiendo a no ser que te gusten los juegos de pulsar botones y brillos bonitos, por lo demas, ni lo compres, 80 euros que la verdad dejan mucho que desear hasta en las animaciones y gestos de personajes principales, parece de ps3 en algunos momentos.
